newsitem.title: UK: Town cryer dissolves parliament for UK election.
newsitem.headline: Town cryer dissolves parliament for UK election.

text.p: The City of London's town cryer, dressed in full court uniform, formally dissolved parliament on Tuesday ahead of the May 1 British election in a ceremony dating back to the 14th century.

Colonel Tommy Tucker, in his capacity as the Common Cryer and Serjeant-at-Arms, stood on the steps of the Royal Exchange building in the financial district of London to announce that, by the order of Queen Elizabeth II, parliament was dissolved.
Tourists reached for their cameras as Tucker, in keeping with tradition, stood in full court dress, wig and gown, in bright sunshine to deliver his message from a scroll.
Before the arrival of newspapers, television, and radio, this was how the citizens of the capital first heard of the dissolution of parliament.
Tucker was led to the steps by a yeoman, who carried his speech. He was accompanied by the Lord Mayor's footman, also in full ceremonial garb, and two City of London police.

The only modern element of the ceremony was the use of a microphone so his voice could carry. Within a minute of starting the start, however, Tucker was interrupted by an ambulance with sirens wailing and had to wait for it to pass.
He began the royal proclamation with the traditional "Oyez Oyez Oyez" to call those gathered to attention and finished with a respectful "God save the Queen".
The speech, written in old English and full of the royal we and words like "hereby", was long and detailed. The first City of London Common Cryer was Thomas de Kent in 1309.

"And we being desirous and resolved, as soon as maybe, to meet our people, and to have their advice in parliament, do hereby make known to all our loving subjects, our royal will and pleasure to call a new parliament," he said quoting the monarch.
Prime Minister John Major called the election on March 17 from the steps of his London residence, 10, Downing Street.
But, this being Britain, things have to be done according to the book and the campaign is not officially considered to be under way until parliament, which has not sat since March 21, is dissolved.
"There's an element of anachronism but it's one of the traditions that are still going on that make London a place to visit," said Corporation of London spokesman Simon Morrison.
Tony Blair's opposition Labour Party is well ahead in the polls and looking like ending 18 years of Conservative rule.

Tucker, born in 1935, has announced the dissolution of parliament twice before in 1987 and 1992. He spent most of his adult life abroad with the Royal Regiment of Artillery in Cyprus, Germany, Northern Ireland, Hong Kong and Uganda. REUTER
